summaries.example: Imagine two statements: “All squares have four sides” and “The playground is wet.” You can think about the first statement and understand why it is true. To know the second, you probably need to look outside or hear from someone who checked. The first is a possible example of a priori justification; the second is a possible example of a posteriori justification.
summaries.summary: A priori justification is a kind of good reason for believing something that does not depend on experience in the usual way. For example, understanding what a square is may help you see that every square has four sides. A posteriori justification, in contrast, depends on experience, such as seeing that the grass is wet. The difference is not always simple. Some truths that seem necessary, such as facts about water, may need scientific investigation. Some statements that could have been different may still be knowable without new observations. Philosophers also ask whether a priori thinking is always reliable, whether it can be defeated by later evidence, and whether it is based on intellectual “seeing,” understanding, reasoning skills, or a default permission to believe. The entry also explains why a true belief with good reasons can still fail to be knowledge when luck is involved.
key_ideas: Some beliefs seem supportable just by understanding an idea or thinking carefully about it.
Other beliefs need observation or information from experience.
Philosophers disagree about whether a priori reasons come from special intellectual insights, ordinary reasoning skills, understanding concepts, or no evidence at all.
A priori justification can be mistaken and can be changed by new reasons or evidence.
Having a justified true belief may not be enough for knowledge, because luck can be involved.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us notice where our reasons come from. It encourages us to separate what we understand from what we have learned by observing. It also teaches that confidence and truth are not always enough: a person may be right for the wrong reason or may need to reconsider a belief when better evidence appears.

important_terms.definition: A reason for believing something that does not depend on observing or experiencing the world, beyond what is needed to understand the ideas involved.
A reason for believing something that depends on seeing, hearing, remembering, or otherwise learning from experience.
A reason that supports a belief. A belief is justified when a person has good reason to hold it.
A statement that can be true or false, such as “Squares have four sides.”
A belief that is true but correct partly by luck, so it may not count as knowledge.

questions_to_think_about: Can you think of a statement you know by understanding it rather than by looking for evidence?
Could careful thinking ever lead someone to a wrong answer?
If new evidence challenges a belief, should the belief always be changed?
Is knowing something different from being right by luck?

summaries.example: Consider “All bachelors are unmarried men” and “Water is H₂O.” The first can appear knowable through the meaning of the term “bachelor,” so it is a candidate for a priori justification. The second is widely treated as requiring empirical discovery, even though it may be necessary—that is, true in every possible situation. This shows why the a priori/a posteriori distinction is not simply the same as the necessary/contingent distinction.
summaries.summary: The entry examines a priori justification, understood as epistemic support that is independent of experience, and contrasts it with a posteriori or empirical justification. Familiar examples suggest that conceptual truths, mathematics, logic, and some moral or modal judgments may be justified by understanding and reflection. Yet the boundaries are contested. Necessary truths such as chemical identities may require empirical discovery, while some contingent propositions have been proposed as knowable a priori. The entry therefore separates questions about what is true in every possible world from questions about how a person is justified in believing it. It also argues that a priori justification need not be infallible or immune to defeat: paradoxes, further reasoning, and even empirical evidence may undermine it. Major accounts locate its basis in rational intuitions, intellectual seemings, conceptual understanding, imaginative skills, or entitlement to accept certain presuppositions without evidence. Critics challenge whether intuitions are genuine evidence, whether they can be calibrated, whether experimental studies measure the relevant phenomenon, and whether empirical investigation should instead determine the nature of knowledge and justification. Finally, the entry considers whether a priori justification can yield knowledge of the external world and whether a priori knowledge requires justification at all.
key_ideas: The usual distinction says that a priori justification does not rely on experience, while a posteriori justification does. But experience may still be needed to acquire concepts or learn difficult reasoning techniques.

The a priori/a posteriori distinction does not map perfectly onto the necessary/contingent distinction. Some necessary truths may require empirical discovery, and some contingent truths have been proposed as knowable a priori.
Analytic propositions are a central, but not exhaustive, class of possible a priori truths. Synthetic a priori propositions are disputed examples.
A priori justification may be fallible and defeasible. Reflection, paradoxes, expert criticism, or empirical information can undermine it.
One influential proposal treats rational intuitions or insights as non-inferential intellectual states that provide evidence. Critics question their content, reliability, calibration, and relevance.

Other views appeal to imagination, conceptual understanding, acquired reasoning skills, default entitlement, or project-relative presuppositions rather than a special nonexperiential evidential source.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction clarifies two different routes to belief: reasoning from concepts and learning from the world. It matters for mathematics, logic, ethics, science, and philosophical method. It also raises a general lesson about knowledge: a belief can be true and well supported yet still fail to qualify as knowledge if luck, unreliable processes, or missing conditions remain. Understanding these disputes helps readers evaluate arguments without treating intuition, certainty, or agreement as automatically decisive.

important_terms.definition: Justification for a belief that is independent of experience, apart from experience needed to acquire the relevant concepts or intellectual skills.
Justification that depends on sensory information, introspection, memory, testimony, or other experience-based sources.
True in virtue of meaning or concept relations, often illustrated by statements that become logical truths after replacing terms with synonyms.
Not true merely because of meaning; in this context, a proposition that may nevertheless be justified independently of experience.
True in every possible world or situation; necessity concerns how things could be, not by itself how we know them.
A type of justification that can support a false belief. Fallibility does not mean the justification is worthless.
Able to be overturned or weakened by later evidence, either because the belief is false or because its supporting reason is undermined.
A case in which a person has a justified true belief but lacks knowledge because the belief is true in an epistemically lucky way.

questions_to_think_about: Does knowing the meaning of a word ever suffice for knowing that a proposition is true?
Why might “Water is H₂O” be necessary yet empirically discoverable?
If a mathematical proof seems convincing but experts find a serious error, what happens to the original justification?
Should philosophers treat intuitive judgments as evidence, or mainly as clues about which concepts to investigate?
Can reliable true belief be knowledge if the believer has no reason to think the method is reliable?

summaries.example: Suppose a friend says, “Every triangle has three sides,” and “The school bus is late today.” You can understand the first claim and reason about it without checking a bus schedule. The second claim needs observation, a message, or some other experience. Philosophers call the first kind of support a possible example of a priori justification and the second a posteriori justification. But the border is not always clear: some scientific truths may be necessary even though we discover them by experiment.
summaries.summary: A priori justification is support for a belief that is independent of experience in the relevant evidential sense. Understanding a concept, following a proof, or reflecting on a claim may be enough. A posteriori justification depends on experience, including observation, memory, testimony, or information about the world. The distinction raises several puzzles. Necessary truths are often thought to be a priori, but some necessary claims—such as claims about the chemical nature of substances—may be discovered empirically. Conversely, philosophers have proposed contingent claims that can be known a priori. The entry also asks whether a priori justification is certain. It presents reasons for thinking that it can be mistaken and defeated by later evidence. Competing theories say that its basis is conceptual understanding, rational intuition, imaginative comparison, acquired intellectual skills, default reasonableness, or rational permission to accept certain assumptions for a project. Critics question whether these sources truly provide evidence and whether studying people’s intuitive judgments can settle philosophical questions. The discussion ends by asking whether a priori justification can produce knowledge about the external world and whether knowledge itself must be analyzed using justification.
key_ideas: A priori and a posteriori describe different ways a belief may be supported, not simply two groups of true statements.
Philosophers debate whether a priori knowledge concerns only necessary truths. Examples involving measurement, identity, and self-location suggest that the issue is more complicated.
A priori reasoning can go wrong. A person may overlook a counterexample, misunderstand a concept, or accept several claims that conflict with one another.
Some philosophers think rational intuitions provide evidence; others think they are ordinary mental responses, useful clues, or unreliable guides.
A person may be allowed to accept a starting assumption for an investigation without having evidence for it. Whether that counts as a priori justification is disputed.
Knowledge may require more than a justified true belief, because a lucky success is not always knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue affects how we judge arguments in school, science, mathematics, and everyday life. It reminds us that “I can imagine it” and “I observed it” are different kinds of support. It also encourages intellectual humility: even careful reasoning can contain hidden assumptions, and new evidence may show that a belief needs revision.

important_terms.definition: A good reason for believing a claim that does not depend on new observations, though learning the relevant words or skills may require experience.
A good reason for believing a claim that comes from observation, memory, testimony, or another experience-based source.
A claim that can be true or false. Philosophers use this word for statements such as “Every triangle has three sides.”
True because of meanings or logical structure, rather than because of a special fact discovered about the world.
A kind of support that can be present even when the belief turns out to be false.
Able to be defeated, weakened, or overturned by additional reasons or evidence.
A situation in which a person has a true belief and some justification, but is correct partly by luck and therefore may not have knowledge.
A mental seeming or insight that a claim is true, possible, or necessary, without reaching it through an explicit argument.

questions_to_think_about: Is “Every triangle has three sides” known in a different way from “The sidewalk is icy”?
Can a belief based on careful reasoning still be false?
What kind of evidence could show that an intellectual intuition is trustworthy?
Should a scientific discovery ever count as a priori knowledge if the truth discovered is necessary?
What extra condition might separate knowledge from a lucky, justified true belief?
